analysis.one_liner: Eliminates Medicare drug copays and coinsurance once a senior's yearly out-of-pocket drug costs hit the cap.
analysis.headline: The bill to end Medicare drug cost-sharing above the catastrophic threshold died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote or a hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Medicare's prescription drug benefit, seniors and people with disabilities who reach the annual out-of-pocket limit still keep paying copays or coinsurance on every refill. This bill would have ended that, starting in 2018, so once a beneficiary hit the yearly cap the plan would cover the rest with nothing out of pocket. It was introduced by Sen. Wyden in April 2016, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly several million Medicare beneficiaries each year who take expensive drugs — people with cancer, hepatitis C, rheumatoid arthritis, and other costly conditions — would stop paying 5% coinsurance on every prescription after hitting the out-of-pocket cap, protection that could save them thousands of dollars a year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on expensive Medicare drug plans

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates beneficiary cost-sharing — copays and coinsurance — above the Medicare prescription drug benefit's annual out-of-pocket threshold starting in plan year 2018, so after the cap is reached, prescriptions cost nothing more [S2][S3].

The bill targets people who need the most medication: those who spend past the cap in a given year are typically managing expensive chronic conditions, and today they keep paying coinsurance on every refill even after the plan's own protection supposedly kicks in [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Part D plan sponsors — the private insurers that run the drug plans — would bear the full cost of every prescription above the cap without any new federal funding in the bill, a cost they would likely pass to all beneficiaries through higher monthly premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill provides no new federal funding, so the added cost of fully covering drugs above the cap would fall on Part D plan sponsors and likely reappear as higher premiums spread across all beneficiaries, including those who never reach the cap [S3].

Ending cost-sharing removes any price signal at the pharmacy counter, which some critics argue could increase overuse of higher-priced drugs; the bill caps what patients pay without touching the underlying drug prices that push people past the cap in the first place [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the beneficiaries with the highest drug costs — often people with cancer or other serious illnesses — the protection is real and large, ending open-ended coinsurance. The cost is real too: with no dedicated funding source, the expense shifts to plans and premiums, and the bill does nothing about the high drug prices that create the problem. A well-designed version would pair the cap with a funding mechanism or price negotiation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2016, and the committee never took it up; when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017, the bill died.

narrative.text: Sen. Wyden introduced the bill on April 27, 2016, joined by Democratic cosponsors including Sens. Cardin, Bennet, and Cantwell [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and that was the last action of any kind in its history [S5].
It gathered 7 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 44 Senate Democrats [S4].
No hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Part D plan sponsors benefited, since they never had to absorb the full cost of prescriptions above the out-of-pocket cap. Seniors and disabled beneficiaries with the highest drug costs kept paying coinsurance on every refill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Part D insurers; sick seniors kept paying

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plan sponsors (private insurers)
industries.note: Starting in 2018, plans would have to cover 100% of prescription costs above the annual out-of-pocket cap with no new federal money, ending the copays and coinsurance patients currently pay. Their savings come directly at the cost of protection for the sickest beneficiaries, and any added cost would likely show up in premiums for everyone.

With cost-sharing eliminated above the cap, patients would be more likely to fill every prescription and drug makers would be paid in full without the deterrence of coinsurance. But the same high list prices that push patients past the cap would continue untouched.
